Expect the routes `supervisor`, `return-policy`, `standard-refund`, `defective-exchange`, `standard-exchange` and `generic`. A large refund matches the first case even when it is also late, because only the first matching case is selected.

## Default Fallback

Always include a default condition as the last one in your switch task to ensure the workflow always has a path forward:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: default-fallback
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - checkOrderStatus:
      switch:
        - approved:
            when: ${ .status == "approved" }
            then: processApprovedOrder
        - pending:
            when: ${ .status == "pending" }
            then: waitForApproval
        - rejected:
            when: ${ .status == "rejected" }
            then: handleRejectedOrder
        - unknown:
            then: handleUnknownStatus
  - processApprovedOrder:
      set:
        next: ship
      then: exit
  - waitForApproval:
      set:
        next: wait
      then: exit
  - handleRejectedOrder:
      set:
        next: cancel
      then: exit
  - handleUnknownStatus:
      set:
        next: investigate
```

Save it as `default-fallback.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f default-fallback.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples default-fallback --input '{"status":"approved"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples default-fallback --input '{"status":"pending"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples default-fallback --input '{"status":"rejected"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples default-fallback --input '{"status":"lost"}'
```

Expect `ship`, `wait`, `cancel` and, for the unexpected status, `investigate`. The last case has no `when`, so it always matches: there's always a path, even if none of the explicit conditions match.

## Working with Arrays and Objects

jq expressions can work with complex data structures. This example chooses a shipping method from item weights, the shipping preferences and the customer tier:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: working-with-arrays-and-objects
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - determineShippingMethod:
      switch:
        - heavy:
            when: ${ .items | map(.weight) | add > 20 }
            then: arrangeFreightShipping
        - express:
            when: ${ .shipping.express == true }
            then: arrangeExpressShipping
        - premium:
            when: ${ .customer.tier == "premium" }
            then: arrangePriorityShipping
        - standard:
            then: arrangeStandardShipping
  - arrangeFreightShipping:
      set:
        shipping: freight
      then: exit
  - arrangeExpressShipping:
      set:
        shipping: express
      then: exit
  - arrangePriorityShipping:
      set:
        shipping: priority
      then: exit
  - arrangeStandardShipping:
      set:
        shipping: standard
```

Save it as `working-with-arrays-and-objects.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f working-with-arrays-and-objects.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples working-with-arrays-and-objects --input '{"items":[{"weight":15},{"weight":10}]}'
bin/lemline instance start examples working-with-arrays-and-objects --input '{"items":[{"weight":2}],"shipping":{"express":true}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples working-with-arrays-and-objects --input '{"items":[{"weight":2}],"customer":{"tier":"premium"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples working-with-arrays-and-objects --input '{"items":[{"weight":2}]}'
```

Expect `freight`, `express`, `priority` and `standard`. A missing field such as `.shipping.express` is `null`, so its condition is simply false.

## Combining Multiple Variables

You can reference multiple variables in a single condition:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: combining-multiple-variables
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - applyDiscount:
      switch:
        - premium:
            when: ${ .customer.loyaltyYears >= 5 and .order.total > 100 }
            then: applyPremiumDiscount
        - standard:
            when: ${ .customer.loyaltyYears >= 2 or .order.total > 200 }
            then: applyStandardDiscount
        - sale:
            when: ${ .order.items | map(select(.category == "sale")) | length > 0 }
            then: applySaleDiscount
        - none:
            then: noDiscount
  - applyPremiumDiscount:
      set:
        discountPercent: 20
      then: exit
  - applyStandardDiscount:
      set:
        discountPercent: 10
      then: exit
  - applySaleDiscount:
      set:
        discountPercent: 5
      then: exit
  - noDiscount:
      set:
        discountPercent: 0
```

Save it as `combining-multiple-variables.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f combining-multiple-variables.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-multiple-variables --input '{"customer":{"loyaltyYears":6},"order":{"total":150,"items":[]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-multiple-variables --input '{"customer":{"loyaltyYears":3},"order":{"total":50,"items":[]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-multiple-variables --input '{"customer":{"loyaltyYears":0},"order":{"total":50,"items":[{"category":"sale"}]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-multiple-variables --input '{"customer":{"loyaltyYears":0},"order":{"total":50,"items":[{"category":"garden"}]}}'
```

This example determines discounts based on customer loyalty, order total, and item categories. Expect `discountPercent` 20, 10, 5 and 0.

## Nested Decision Making

For complex decision making, you can use multiple switch tasks in sequence:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: nested-decision-making
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - evaluateRiskLevel:
      switch:
        - highValue:
            when: ${ .transaction.amount > 10000 }
            then: highValueCheck
        - other:
            then: standardCheck
  - highValueCheck:
      switch:
        - flagged:
            when: ${ .customer.history.flags | length > 0 }
            then: manualReview
        - established:
            when: ${ .customer.accountAgeDays >= 90 }
            then: autoApprove
        - recent:
            then: additionalVerification
  - manualReview:
      set:
        decision: manual-review
      then: exit
  - additionalVerification:
      set:
        decision: verification
      then: exit
  - autoApprove:
      set:
        decision: approved
      then: exit
  - standardCheck:
      set:
        decision: standard
```

Save it as `nested-decision-making.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f nested-decision-making.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples nested-decision-making --input '{"transaction":{"amount":20000},"customer":{"history":{"flags":["chargeback"]},"accountAgeDays":400}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples nested-decision-making --input '{"transaction":{"amount":20000},"customer":{"history":{"flags":[]},"accountAgeDays":400}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples nested-decision-making --input '{"transaction":{"amount":20000},"customer":{"history":{"flags":[]},"accountAgeDays":10}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples nested-decision-making --input '{"transaction":{"amount":500}}'
```

This example implements a two-level decision tree for risk evaluation. Expect the decisions `manual-review`, `approved`, `verification` and `standard`.

## Using Data Transformations before Switching

You can use a `set` task to prepare data for a switch decision:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: using-data-transformations-before-switching
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - prepareDecisionData:
      set:
        isNewCustomer: ${ (.orderDate | fromdateiso8601) - (.customer.joinDate | fromdateiso8601) < 30 * 24 * 3600 }
        isHighValue: ${ .order.total > 1000 }
        hasRiskyItems: ${ .order.items | map(select(.category == "restricted")) | length > 0 }
  - routeOrder:
      switch:
        - restricted:
            when: ${ .hasRiskyItems == true }
            then: complianceReview
        - newAndLarge:
            when: ${ .isNewCustomer == true and .isHighValue == true }
            then: verificationProcess
        - large:
            when: ${ .isHighValue == true }
            then: priorityProcessing
        - other:
            then: standardProcessing
  - complianceReview:
      set:
        route: compliance
      then: exit
  - verificationProcess:
      set:
        route: verification
      then: exit
  - priorityProcessing:
      set:
        route: priority
      then: exit
  - standardProcessing:
      set:
        route: standard
```

Save it as `using-data-transformations-before-switching.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f using-data-transformations-before-switching.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples using-data-transformations-before-switching --input '{"orderDate":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z","customer":{"joinDate":"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"},"order":{"total":50,"items":[{"category":"restricted"}]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples using-data-transformations-before-switching --input '{"orderDate":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z","customer":{"joinDate":"2026-02-20T00:00:00Z"},"order":{"total":1500,"items":[]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples using-data-transformations-before-switching --input '{"orderDate":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z","customer":{"joinDate":"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"},"order":{"total":1500,"items":[]}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples using-data-transformations-before-switching --input '{"orderDate":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z","customer":{"joinDate":"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"},"order":{"total":50,"items":[]}}'
```

This pattern improves readability by computing derived values before the switch. A customer is new when they joined less than 30 days before the order date. Expect the routes `compliance`, `verification`, `priority` and `standard`.

## Error Handling in Switch Tasks

If an expression in a condition fails, the switch task raises an expression error. Wrap the expression in jq's `try ... catch false` to treat a failure as `false`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: error-handling-in-switch-tasks
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - processPayment:
      switch:
        - paid:
            when: '${ try (.paymentResult.status == "success") catch false }'
            then: completeOrder
        - pending:
            when: '${ try (.paymentResult.status == "pending") catch false }'
            then: waitForPayment
        - failed:
            then: handlePaymentFailure
  - completeOrder:
      set:
        orderStatus: completed
      then: exit
  - waitForPayment:
      set:
        orderStatus: waiting
      then: exit
  - handlePaymentFailure:
      set:
        orderStatus: payment-failed
```

Save it as `error-handling-in-switch-tasks.yaml` and run one instance per branch:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f error-handling-in-switch-tasks.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples error-handling-in-switch-tasks --input '{"paymentResult":{"status":"success"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples error-handling-in-switch-tasks --input '{"paymentResult":{"status":"pending"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples error-handling-in-switch-tasks --input '{"paymentResult":"timeout"}'
```

Expect `completed`, `waiting` and `payment-failed`. In the third input `paymentResult` is a string: reading `.status` from it fails, `try` turns the failure into `false`, and the default case handles the order.

## Combining Switch with Try/Catch

For robust conditional handling, combine switch with try/catch. This workflow reserves one unit, charges the order
in the shop, then routes on the charge status:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: combining-switch-with-try-catch
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - reserveStock:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/reservations
        body:
          orderId: ${ .orderId }
          items: [{ id: SKU-1, quantity: 1 }]
  - processOrder:
      try:
        - attemptPayment:
            call: http
            with:
              method: post
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/charges
              query:
                fail: '503'
                failTimes: ${ $workflow.input.failures // 0 | tostring }
              body:
                orderId: ${ $workflow.input.orderId }
                paymentInfo:
                  token: ${ $workflow.input.token }
        - evaluatePayment:
            switch:
              - success:
                  when: ${ .status == "approved" }
                  then: completeOrder
              - review:
                  when: ${ .status == "review" }
                  then: flagForReview
              - default:
                  then: handleFailure
        - completeOrder:
            set:
              orderStatus: completed
            then: exit
        - flagForReview:
            set:
              orderStatus: in-review
            then: exit
        - handleFailure:
            set:
              orderStatus: payment-failed
      catch:
        retry:
          delay:
            seconds: 1
          limit:
            attempt:
              count: 3
        do:
          - handleError:
              set:
                orderStatus: error
```

The `switch` routes on the payment result. If the payment call fails, the `catch` retries the `try` block up to
three times, then runs `handleError`. The shop answers `approved` or `review`, so the default case is only a
safeguard. The `failures` input makes the shop answer HTTP 503 that many times before it accepts the charge.
Save it as `combining-switch-with-try-catch.yaml` and run four orders:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f combining-switch-with-try-catch.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-switch-with-try-catch --input '{"orderId":"ORD-501","token":"approved"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-switch-with-try-catch --input '{"orderId":"ORD-502","token":"review"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-switch-with-try-catch --input '{"orderId":"ORD-503","token":"approved","failures":2}'
bin/lemline instance start examples combining-switch-with-try-catch --input '{"orderId":"ORD-504","token":"declined"}'
```

Expect `completed` and `in-review` at once. ORD-503 completes after two retries. ORD-504 is declined with HTTP 402
on every attempt and ends with `{"orderStatus":"error"}` after the third retry. The worker picks up retries every
10 seconds, so allow about a minute for the last two.

## Real-World Example: Order Processing

Here's a complete example of an order processing workflow with multiple decision points. It reserves the stock,
asks both carriers for a quote, applies the customer's shipping choice, charges the payment and books the shipment:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: shop-order-routing
  version: '1.0.0'
  title: Order Processing Workflow
do:
  - validateOrder:
      set:
        isValid: ${ .items | length > 0 }
      output:
        as: '${ $input + . }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
  - checkOrderValidity:
      switch:
        - invalid:
            when: ${ .isValid == false }
            then: rejectOrder
        - valid:
            then: reserveStock
  - reserveStock:
      try:
        - requestReservation:
            call: http
            with:
              method: post
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/reservations
              body:
                orderId: ${ .orderId }
                items: ${ .items }
            output:
              as: '${ { reserved: true, reservationId: .id } }'
      catch:
        do:
          - markUnavailable:
              set:
                reserved: false
      output:
        as: '${ $context.order + . }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
  - evaluateInventory:
      switch:
        - available:
            when: ${ .reserved == true }
            then: getQuotes
        - unavailable:
            then: handleOutOfStock
  - getQuotes:
      fork:
        branches:
          - express:
              call: http
              with:
                method: post
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/express
                body:
                  orderId: ${ .orderId }
          - economy:
              call: http
              with:
                method: post
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/economy
                body:
                  orderId: ${ .orderId }
      output:
        as: '${ $context.order + { quotes: . } }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
  - determineShippingMethod:
      switch:
        - express:
            when: ${ .express == true }
            then: applyExpressShipping
        - economy:
            then: applyEconomyShipping
  - applyExpressShipping:
      set:
        carrier: express
        shippingCost: ${ .quotes | map(select(.carrier == "express")) | .[0].price }
      output:
        as: '${ $context.order + . }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
      then: processPayment
  - applyEconomyShipping:
      set:
        carrier: economy
        shippingCost: ${ .quotes | map(select(.carrier == "economy")) | .[0].price }
      output:
        as: '${ $context.order + . }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
  - processPayment:
      try:
        - charge:
            call: http
            with:
              method: post
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/charges
              body:
                orderId: ${ .orderId }
                paymentInfo: ${ .paymentInfo }
      catch:
        do:
          - markDeclined:
              set:
                status: declined
      output:
        as: '${ $context.order + { payment: . } }'
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { order: . } }'
  - evaluatePayment:
      switch:
        - approved:
            when: ${ .payment.status == "approved" }
            then: bookShipment
        - review:
            when: ${ .payment.status == "review" }
            then: flagForReview
        - declined:
            then: handleDeclinedPayment
  - bookShipment:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/shipments
        body:
          orderId: ${ .orderId }
          carrier: ${ .carrier }
  - completeOrder:
      set:
        orderStatus: CONFIRMED
        message: ${ "Your order has been confirmed and will ship via " + .carrier + "." }
      then: end
  - rejectOrder:
      set:
        orderStatus: REJECTED
        message: Your order could not be processed because it contains no items.
      then: end
  - handleOutOfStock:
      set:
        orderStatus: REJECTED
        message: Your order could not be processed because some items are out of stock.
      then: end
  - flagForReview:
      set:
        orderStatus: PENDING_REVIEW
        message: Your order requires additional review. We will contact you shortly.
      then: end
  - handleDeclinedPayment:
      set:
        orderStatus: PAYMENT_DECLINED
        message: Your payment was declined. Please try a different payment method.
```

A task replaces the data it received with its own result. To keep the order available to later tasks, each task that produces data merges its result into the order kept in `$context.order`.
Save it as `real-world-example-order-processing.yaml` and run one order per outcome:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f real-world-example-order-processing.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-601","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":1}],"express":true,"paymentInfo":{"token":"approved"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-602","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":1}],"express":false,"paymentInfo":{"token":"approved"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-603","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":1}],"express":false,"paymentInfo":{"token":"review"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-604","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":1}],"express":false,"paymentInfo":{"token":"declined"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-605","items":[],"paymentInfo":{"token":"approved"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples shop-order-routing --input '{"orderId":"ORD-606","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":500}],"paymentInfo":{"token":"approved"}}'
```

| Order |Expected `orderStatus` |What the shop shows |
------------------------------------------------------
| ORD-601 |`CONFIRMED`, message ending `ship via express.` |Reservation, approved charge, express shipment |
| ORD-602 |`CONFIRMED`, message ending `ship via economy.` |Reservation, approved charge, economy shipment |
| ORD-603 |`PENDING_REVIEW` |Reservation and a charge with status `review`, no shipment |
| ORD-604 |`PAYMENT_DECLINED` |Reservation and a declined charge, no shipment |
| ORD-605 |`REJECTED`, no items |Nothing |
| ORD-606 |`REJECTED`, out of stock |Nothing: the shop refuses the reservation with HTTP 409 |

This example does not release the stock of orders that are not shipped. See
[the compensation example](lemline-example-compensation.html) for that. Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

## Best Practices for Switch Tasks

1. Order conditions from specific to general: Put more specific conditions first

2. Always include a default case: End the switch with a case that has no `when`

3. Preprocess data when needed: Use a `set` task before complex switching

4. Keep conditions readable: Break complex conditions into separate variables

5. Avoid deep nesting: Prefer multiple sequential switch tasks over deeply nested logic

6. Use meaningful task names: Name tasks according to the decision they represent

7. Handle all edge cases: Consider what happens if data is missing or unexpected

8. Document complex logic: Add comments explaining business rules

## Next Steps

* Learn about [executing tasks in parallel](lemline-howto-parallel.html)

* Explore [running loops in workflows](lemline-howto-loops.html)

* Understand [how to use try/catch for error handling](lemline-howto-try-catch.html)



# How to execute tasks in parallel

Use `fork.branches` to run independent branches concurrently. Each branch has its own
task input. By default, a fork waits for all branches.

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Run the commands from a second
terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The examples
call the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop); start it from the root of
the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

Save this definition as `parallel-order-checks.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: parallel-order-checks
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - checkOrder:
      fork:
        branches:
          - checkStock:
              call: http
              with:
                method: get
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              output:
                as: '${ { available: .available } }'
          - checkShipping:
              call: http
              with:
                method: post
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/express
                body: ${ . }
      output:
        as: '${ { checks: . } }'
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f parallel-order-checks.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples parallel-order-checks --input '{"orderId":"QUOTE-1"}'
```

The fork returns the results of its branches in the order they are listed:
`{"checks":[{"available":100},{"orderId":"QUOTE-1","carrier":"express","attempts":1,"price":9}]}`.
For a complete checkout, [compare the two carriers](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#ship-a-paid-order). Each branch returns its own price and `min_by(.price)` selects the carrier after both branches finish.

## Handle errors around a fork

Use a surrounding `try` task when the workflow needs a fallback for the whole group.
Place a separate `try` inside a branch when that branch can recover independently.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: parallel-checks-with-fallback
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - attemptChecks:
      try:
        - checkOrder:
            fork:
              branches:
                - inventory:
                    call: http
                    with:
                      method: get
                      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
                      query:
                        fail: '503'
                        failTimes: ${ .inventoryFailures // 0 | tostring }
                        key: ${ .orderId }
                - shipping:
                    call: http
                    with:
                      method: post
                      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/express
                      body:
                        orderId: ${ .orderId }
      catch:
        do:
          - requestManualReview:
              set:
                status: needs-review
```

The `inventoryFailures` input makes the shop's stock endpoint answer HTTP 503 that many times. Save the
definition as `parallel-checks-with-fallback.yaml` and run it with a working and a failing inventory:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f parallel-checks-with-fallback.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples parallel-checks-with-fallback --input '{"orderId":"QUOTE-2"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples parallel-checks-with-fallback --input '{"orderId":"QUOTE-3","inventoryFailures":1}'
```

The first instance returns both branch results. In the second, the inventory branch fails, the fork fails with it,
and the `catch` returns `{"status":"needs-review"}`. The shipping branch still ran: the shop lists an express quote for `QUOTE-3`.

## Wait for outcomes published as events

A `listen` task can collect events produced by independent services. In this example,
`all` requires one match for each filter and `timeout.after` bounds the wait.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: listen-for-all-results
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - collectResults:
      listen:
        to:
          all:
            - with:
                type: com.example.inventory.checked
            - with:
                type: com.example.shipping.quoted
      timeout:
        after: PT5M
  - recordResults:
      set:
        checks: ${ . }
```

This example needs the publisher from the tutorial. Save it as `tutorial-publisher.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: tutorial-publisher
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - publish:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: ${ .type }
            source: https://events.example.com/tutorial
            data: ${ .data }
```

Save the listener as `listen-for-all-results.yaml`, start it, then publish both events:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f tutorial-publisher.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f listen-for-all-results.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples listen-for-all-results
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.inventory.checked","data":{"stock":2}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.shipping.quoted","data":{"price":15}}'
```

After the second event the listener completes with `{"checks":[{"stock":2},{"price":15}]}`. Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

Use a [For Task](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#for) to iterate over a collection at runtime. See
[Fan-Out and Fan-In](lemline-explain-fan-in.html) for the difference between iteration,
forking tasks and waiting for events.



# How to run loops (for, while)

Use a `for` task to iterate over an array. The `in` expression selects the collection,
`each` binds an item and `at` binds its index. The body is a nested `do` list.

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Run the commands from a second
terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The worker logs
`Workflow completed with output` with each result. Save each definition under the file name used in its
`definition post` command.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: map-order-items
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - calculateTotals:
      for:
        each: item
        in: ${ .items }
        at: index
      do:
        - calculateLine:
            set:
              itemId: ${ $item.id }
              index: ${ $index }
              lineTotal: ${ $item.quantity * $item.price }
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f map-order-items.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples map-order-items --input '{"items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":2,"price":25},{"id":"SKU-2","quantity":1,"price":12}]}'
```

The body runs once per item, but the `for` task returns only the last iteration's result:
`{"itemId":"SKU-2","index":1,"lineTotal":12}`. To keep every line, collect them as shown next.

## Collect a result across iterations

Lemline passes one iteration's result into the next iteration. Initialize an
accumulator, then update it in the body. The last iteration's result becomes the
loop result. Here the body adds a line total for each input item.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: collect-order-lines
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  from: '${ { lines: [] } }'
do:
  - calculateLines:
      for:
        each: item
        in: ${ $workflow.input.items }
      do:
        - appendLine:
            set:
              lines: '${ .lines + [{ id: $item.id, amount: ($item.price * $item.quantity) }] }'
```

The workflow's `input.from` starts the loop with an empty `lines` array. Each iteration receives the previous one's
result and appends a line.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f collect-order-lines.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples collect-order-lines --input '{"items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":2,"price":25},{"id":"SKU-2","quantity":1,"price":12}]}'
```

Expect `{"lines":[{"id":"SKU-1","amount":50},{"id":"SKU-2","amount":12}]}`.

## Stop a loop early

Add a `while` condition to the same task when the loop should stop before the
collection is exhausted. See the [For Task](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#for) for the condition and
its scope. Use a [fork](lemline-howto-parallel.html) for independent concurrent branches.



# How to jump between tasks (then, exit, end)

Tasks run in the order listed in `do`. Use a flow directive to override that order.

| Directive |Effect |
---------------------
| `continue` |Advance to the next task in the current list |
| Task name |Move to the named task in the current list |
| `exit` |Leave the current task list and return to its parent |
| `end` |End the workflow |

## Select a task with switch

Each named case has a `then` directive. The first case whose `when` condition matches
wins. A final case without a condition provides a fallback.

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Run the commands from a second
terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The worker logs
`Workflow completed with output` with each result. Save each definition under the file name used in its
`definition post` command.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: validate-and-route-order
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  schema:
    format: json
    document:
      type: object
      required: [orderId, total]
      properties:
        orderId:
          type: string
        total:
          type: number
          minimum: 0
do:
  - routeOrder:
      switch:
        - largeOrder:
            when: ${ .total >= 1000 }
            then: requestReview
        - automatic:
            then: acceptOrder
  - requestReview:
      set:
        status: needs-review
      then: exit
  - acceptOrder:
      set:
        status: accepted
output:
  as: '${ { orderId: $workflow.input.orderId, status: .status } }'
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f validate-and-route-order.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples validate-and-route-order --input '{"orderId":"ORD-301","total":250}'
bin/lemline instance start examples validate-and-route-order --input '{"orderId":"ORD-302","total":1500}'
```

Expect `{"orderId":"ORD-301","status":"accepted"}` and `{"orderId":"ORD-302","status":"needs-review"}`.

After setting its status, the manual-review path uses `then: exit` to leave the task list
instead of falling through to the automatic path. The workflow's `output.as` still runs, as it does after `then: end`.

## Exit a nested task list

Here a missing order ID exits the inner `do` list. The outer list resumes at `finalize`.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: exit-nested-scope
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - processOrder:
      do:
        - checkOrder:
            switch:
              - invalid:
                  when: ${ .orderId == null }
                  then: exit
              - valid:
                  then: recordOrder
        - recordOrder:
            set:
              status: received
  - finalize:
      set:
        completed: true
        status: ${ .status // "skipped" }
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f exit-nested-scope.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples exit-nested-scope --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples exit-nested-scope
```

With an order ID, `recordOrder` runs and the result is `{"completed":true,"status":"received"}`. Without one,
the inner list exits before `recordOrder` and the result is `{"completed":true,"status":"skipped"}`.

See [Flow Control](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl.md#task-flow) for task and workflow completion behavior.



# How to call an HTTP service

Set `call: http` and configure the HTTP `method` and `endpoint` under `with`.

The examples call the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop). Complete
[the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Start the shop from the root of the
Lemline source checkout, then run the other commands from a second terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR,
substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

Save this definition as `check-stock.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: check-stock
  version: '0.1.0'
  title: Check the shop stock
do:
  - getStock:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f check-stock.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples check-stock
```

The response body becomes the task output: `{"sku":"SKU-1","available":100,"reserved":0}`.

## Build the request

Use `headers` and `query` for request headers and query parameters. For a POST or
PUT request, supply `body` as a value or a workflow expression. See the
[HTTP Task Reference](lemline-ref-http.html) for request options and output modes.

## Use a dynamic endpoint

Use a jq expression for the complete endpoint when it depends on task input.
Escape an input value before inserting it into the URL path.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: dynamic-http-endpoint
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - getProduct:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: '${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/\(.productId | @uri)" }'
```

Save it as `dynamic-http-endpoint.yaml` and read one known and one unknown product:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f dynamic-http-endpoint.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples dynamic-http-endpoint --input '{"productId":"SKU-2"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples dynamic-http-endpoint --input '{"productId":"SKU 404"}'
```

The first instance returns the watering can, `{"id":"SKU-2","name":"Watering can","category":"garden","price":12,"available":10}`.
For the second, `@uri` sends `/products/SKU%20404`; the shop answers HTTP 404 and the workflow faults with a
`communication` error, status 404, whose title starts with `HTTP 404`. Write path templates such as `{productId}` as an expression like
this one: Lemline does not expand URI templates.

## Authenticate

Use a service-specific header or query parameter for an [API key](lemline-howto-api-keys.html).
Use an endpoint authentication policy for [basic or bearer authentication](lemline-ref-auth.html).

## Recover from an HTTP error

Wrap the call in a `try` task, select the errors to handle in `catch`, and add a retry policy or a fallback list
where appropriate. A failed HTTP call raises a `communication` error whose `status` is the HTTP status and whose title
is `HTTP <code>: <body>`.
Match it with `catch.errors.with`, as here.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: retry-and-fallback
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  retries:
    transient:
      delay: PT2S
      backoff:
        exponential: {}
      limit:
        attempt:
          count: 3
do:
  - fetchInventory:
      try:
        - requestInventory:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              query:
                fail: '503'
                failTimes: ${ .failures // 0 | tostring }
                key: ${ $workflow.id }
      catch:
        errors:
          with:
            type: https://open-workflow-specification.org/spec/1.0.0/errors/communication
            status: 503
        retry: transient
        do:
          - useCachedInventory:
              set:
                inventory: []
                stale: true
```

The `failures` input makes the shop answer HTTP 503 that many times. Save the definition as `retry-and-fallback.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f retry-and-fallback.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples retry-and-fallback --input '{"failures":1}'
bin/lemline instance start examples retry-and-fallback --input '{"failures":5}'
```

The first instance returns the stock after one retry. The second fails four times, then returns
`{"inventory":[],"stale":true}`. Allow about a minute: the worker picks up delayed retries every 10 seconds.
Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

Run [the checkout workflow](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html) to see request bodies, HTTP failure handling and idempotent release against a local service.



# How to describe an OpenAPI call

Open Workflow defines `call: openapi`. Lemline registers such a definition, but it has no OpenAPI executor yet:
an instance faults at the OpenAPI task with `Unknown task type: CallOpenAPI`. Until it does, call the operation
with [an HTTP task](lemline-howto-http.html), as shown at the end of this page. See
[Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html).

## Prepare the example

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Start the
[tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the Lemline source
checkout; it publishes an OpenAPI document of its catalog at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/openapi.json`. Run the other
commands from a second terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

## Choose an operation

Set `with.document.endpoint` to the OpenAPI document, select an operation using
`operationId`, and pass its parameters in `parameters`.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: openapi-list-products
  version: '0.1.0'
do:
  - findGardenProducts:
      call: openapi
      with:
        document:
          endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/openapi.json
        operationId: listProducts
        parameters:
          category: garden
```

Save it as `basic-openapi-call.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f basic-openapi-call.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples openapi-list-products
```

The definition registers. The instance faults with a `runtime` error titled `Unknown task type: CallOpenAPI`.

## Call the same operation over HTTP

The `listProducts` operation is `GET /products` with a `category` query parameter. This HTTP task sends the same request:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: openapi-alternative
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - findGardenProducts:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/products
        query:
          category: garden
        output: content
```

Save it as `alternative.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f alternative.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples openapi-alternative
```

The instance completes with the first page of garden products: `items` lists SKU-1, SKU-2 and SKU-3, and `hasMore`
is `false`. Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

See the [OpenAPI Task](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#openapi-call) for configuration options.



# How to run scripts or containers

Open Workflow defines a `run` task for shell commands, scripts, containers and child
workflows. See [Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html) for Lemline's
runtime support for each variant.

## Prepare the examples

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Run the commands from a second
terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The script
example needs Python 3.8 or later on the worker's machine (`python3` on the path, or `LEMLINE_PYTHON_EXEC` set).

## Run an inline script

Put the script in `run.script.code`, set `language` (`python` or `js`) and pass inputs as named `arguments`.
Lemline writes the code to a temporary file and starts it with each argument as a name followed by its value, so the
script below reads `sys.argv` as pairs. With `return: stdout`, the task output is what the script prints.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: inline-email-check
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - validateEmail:
      run:
        script:
          language: python
          code: |
            import re
            import sys
            args = dict(zip(sys.argv[1::2], sys.argv[2::2]))
            valid = re.fullmatch(r"[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+", args["email"])
            print("valid" if valid else "invalid")
          arguments:
            email: ${ .email }
        return: stdout
```

Save it as `inline-email-check.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f inline-email-check.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples inline-email-check --input '{"email":"ada@example.com"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples inline-email-check --input '{"email":"not-an-email"}'
```

The instances complete with the printed line as a string, `"valid"` and then `"invalid"`.

## Load an external script

Use `run.script.source.endpoint` to reference a script instead of inlining it. Lemline reads the script from the file
system of the runner that executes the task: use an absolute `file://` URI and place the script at that path on every
runner. This example reads it from `/tmp/lemline-scripts`; on Windows, use a path such as `file:///C:/lemline-scripts/email-validator.py`.

Create the script with the same email check as above:

```BASH
mkdir -p /tmp/lemline-scripts
cat > /tmp/lemline-scripts/email-validator.py <<'EOF'
import re
import sys
args = dict(zip(sys.argv[1::2], sys.argv[2::2]))
valid = re.fullmatch(r"[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+", args["email"])
print("valid" if valid else "invalid")
EOF
```

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: load-external-script
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - validateEmail:
      run:
        script:
          language: python
          source:
            endpoint: file:///tmp/lemline-scripts/email-validator.py
          arguments:
            email: ${ .email }
        return: stdout
```

Save it as `load-external-script.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f load-external-script.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples load-external-script --input '{"email":"ada@example.com"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples load-external-script --input '{"email":"not-an-email"}'
```

The instances complete with `valid` and `invalid`. A `source.endpoint` that is not a `file://` URI faults with
`Unsupported scheme for script source`.

The endpoint is either a plain string or an object with a `uri` property. Both accept a
runtime expression, for example `endpoint: ${ .scriptUri }`.

The runner needs Node.js 22 or later for `js` scripts and Python 3.8 or later for `python`
scripts.

## Run a container

Set `run.container.image` and, if needed, a `command` and `volumes`.
The referenced volume path has to be available to the executor.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: run-container-with-volume
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - listReports:
      run:
        container:
          image: alpine:3.22
          command: ls /reports
          volumes:
            /host/reports: /reports
        return: stdout
```

Tip:

Runtime support: Lemline accepts this definition but has no container executor yet. The task fails with
`Unknown run task type: RunContainer`. Use an inline script, or call a service over HTTP, instead.

Save it as `run-container-with-volume.yaml` to see the failure:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f run-container-with-volume.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples run-container-with-volume
```

## Invoke a child workflow

Identify the child by namespace, name and version. Use `run.workflow.input`
to supply named values for the child workflow. Register the child definition before
starting the parent. This child asks the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop)
for an economy quote. Start the shop from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

Save the child as `shipping-quote.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: shipping-quote
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - requestQuote:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/economy
        body:
          orderId: ${ .orderId }
      output:
        as: '${ { orderId: .orderId, carrier: .carrier, price: .price } }'
```

The parent waits for the child and receives its output. Save it as `invoke-order-workflow.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: invoke-order-workflow
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - calculateShipping:
      run:
        workflow:
          namespace: examples
          name: shipping-quote
          version: '1.0.0'
          input:
            orderId: ${ .orderId }
  - recordQuote:
      set:
        quote: ${ . }
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f shipping-quote.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f invoke-order-workflow.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples invoke-order-workflow --input '{"orderId":"ORD-42"}'
```

The parent completes with the child's quote, `{"quote":{"orderId":"ORD-42","carrier":"economy","price":5}}`, and
the shop lists one economy quote for `ORD-42`. Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

See [Run Workflow](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#workflow-process) for awaiting completion and handling results.



# How to describe a gRPC call

Open Workflow defines `call: grpc`. Lemline registers such a definition, but it has no gRPC executor yet: an
instance faults at the gRPC task with `Unknown task type: CallGRPC`. The examples below describe a stock service of
the tutorial shop that exists only as an illustration: the shop has no gRPC server. Until Lemline supports gRPC,
call an HTTP equivalent of the service, as shown at the end of this page. See
[Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html).

To check the registration, complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), keep its worker running and use a
second terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

## Define a unary call

Identify the protobuf resource, service and method. Set `arguments` to the request
message fields.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: grpc-get-stock
  version: '0.1.0'
do:
  - getStock:
      call: grpc
      with:
        proto:
          endpoint: file:///opt/shop/inventory.proto
        service:
          name: shop.InventoryService
          host: localhost
          port: 50051
        method: GetStock
        arguments:
          sku: ${ .sku }
```

Save it as `basic-grpc-call.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f basic-grpc-call.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples grpc-get-stock --input '{"sku":"SKU-1"}'
```

The definition registers. The instance faults with a `runtime` error titled `Unknown task type: CallGRPC`.

## Configure authentication

Attach a policy to the service where the executing runtime supports it. This one sends a bearer token read from the
`apiToken` secret:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: grpc-auth-example
  version: '0.1.0'
use:
  secrets:
    - apiToken
  authentications:
    inventoryAuth:
      bearer:
        token: ${ $secrets.apiToken }
do:
  - getStock:
      call: grpc
      with:
        proto:
          endpoint: file:///opt/shop/inventory.proto
        service:
          name: shop.InventoryService
          host: localhost
          port: 50051
          authentication:
            use: inventoryAuth
        method: GetStock
        arguments:
          sku: ${ .sku }
  - recordStock:
      set:
        checked: true
```

Save it as `example-using-authentication.yaml`. Register it to check the definition; it cannot run on Lemline either:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f example-using-authentication.yaml
```

## Call an HTTP equivalent

Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the
Lemline source checkout. Its product endpoint returns the same stock information over HTTP:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: grpc-alternative
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - getStock:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: '${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/\(.sku | @uri)" }'
```

Save it as `alternative.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f alternative.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples grpc-alternative --input '{"sku":"SKU-1"}'
```

The instance completes with the product and its stock, `{"id":"SKU-1","name":"Garden hose","category":"garden","price":25,"available":100}`.
Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

See the [gRPC Task](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#grpc-call) for configuration fields.



# How to emit and listen for events

An `emit` task publishes a CloudEvent. A `listen` task resumes an existing workflow when
the selected event filters match. To start independent instances on matching events,
configure `schedule.on` at the workflow level.

## Prepare the examples

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html). Run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR,
substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The examples need no shop: events travel on the worker's
SQLite event channel. This publisher sends the event type and data given as its input. Save it as
`tutorial-publisher.yaml` (skip it if you registered it in the tutorial):

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: tutorial-publisher
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - publish:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: ${ .type }
            source: https://events.example.com/tutorial
            data: ${ .data }
```

Save the four definitions of this page under the file names used below and register them all before you start the
worker, so that it loads the event-started workflow of the last section. If the setup worker is running, stop it with Ctrl+C first.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f tutorial-publisher.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f emit-order-created.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f listen-for-payment.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f listen-until-complete.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f order-event-schedule.yaml
bin/lemline listen --debug
```

Run the commands of each section from a second terminal in the setup directory.

## Emit an order event

Set the CloudEvent type and source in `emit.event.with`. You can include business data
in `data` and use `subject` to identify the business entity.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: emit-order-created
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - notifyOrderCreated:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: com.example.order.created
            source: https://events.example.com/order-service
            subject: ${ .orderId }
            data: ${ . }
```

Save it as `emit-order-created.yaml`. It emits `com.example.order.created`, the event that starts the workflow of
[the last section](#start-a-workflow-on-an-event):

```BASH
bin/lemline instance start examples emit-order-created --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1001"}'
```

The emitting instance completes at once. About 10 seconds later, the worker logs a new `order-event-schedule`
instance that completes with `{"orderId":"ORD-1001","status":"received"}`: the worker picks up events for
event-started workflows every 10 seconds.

## Wait for a correlated event

Use `listen.to.one` to match a single event. Use `correlate` to compare a value taken
from the event with a value from the workflow, such as an order ID. Set `timeout.after`
to bound the wait.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: listen-for-payment
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - awaitPayment:
      listen:
        to:
          one:
            with:
              type: com.example.payment.received
            correlate:
              orderId:
                from: ${ .orderId }
                expect: ${ $workflow.input.orderId }
      timeout:
        after: PT30M
```

Save it as `listen-for-payment.yaml`. Start a listener for `ORD-123`, then publish a payment for another order and one for `ORD-123`:

```BASH
bin/lemline instance start examples listen-for-payment --input '{"orderId":"ORD-123"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.payment.received","data":{"orderId":"OTHER"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.payment.received","data":{"orderId":"ORD-123"}}'
```

The payment for `OTHER` leaves the listener waiting. The second payment completes it with `[{"orderId":"ORD-123"}]`.

## Collect events and stop on a signal

Use `any` to collect matching updates and `until` to stop listening on a separate
event. Use `all` when every configured filter must match.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: listen-until-complete
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - collectUpdates:
      listen:
        to:
          any:
            - with:
                type: com.example.order.updated
          until:
            one:
              with:
                type: com.example.order.completed
      timeout:
        after: PT30M
```

Save it as `listen-until-complete.yaml`. Start it, send two updates, then the completion signal:

```BASH
bin/lemline instance start examples listen-until-complete
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.order.updated","data":{"step":"packed"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.order.updated","data":{"step":"labelled"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.order.completed","data":{"orderId":"ORD-1002"}}'
```

The instance completes after the completion event with the two collected updates, `[{"step":"packed"},{"step":"labelled"}]`.

## Start a workflow on an event

Use a workflow-level schedule for event-triggered instances.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: order-event-schedule
  version: '1.0.0'
schedule:
  on:
    one:
      with:
        type: com.example.order.created
input:
  from: ${ .[0] }
do:
  - recordOrder:
      set:
        orderId: ${ .orderId }
        status: received
```

Save it as `order-event-schedule.yaml`. Register it before starting the worker, as in [the preparation](#prepare-the-examples):
a workflow with `schedule.on` cannot be started with `instance start`. Each matching event starts a new instance,
whose input is the list of events that started it; the workflow-level `input.from` takes the first one.
The [emit example](#emit-an-order-event) shows it in action.
See [Event Correlation](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#correlation) for the expression scopes involved
and the [Listen Task](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#listen) for matching strategies and read modes.



# How to pass data between tasks

By default, the transformed output of one task becomes the input of the next task.
Use `input.from` when a task needs to select or reshape its input, and `output.as`
when a task needs to adapt its result for the following step.

## Shape input and output

The workflow below transforms its input, calculates a result and returns selected
fields in its output.

Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker running. Run the commands from a second
terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. Save the
definition as `transform-workflow-data.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: transform-workflow-data
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  from: '${ { customer: .user, items: .payload.items } }'
do:
  - summarize:
      set:
        customerId: ${ .customer.id }
        itemCount: ${ .items | length }
output:
  as: '${ { customerId, itemCount } }'
```

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f transform-workflow-data.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples transform-workflow-data --input '{"user":{"id":"C-100","name":"Ada Lovelace"},"payload":{"items":[{"id":"SKU-1"},{"id":"SKU-2"}]}}'
```

The workflow-level `input.from` keeps only `customer` and `items`, the task counts the items, and `output.as` keeps
two fields: expect `{"customerId":"C-100","itemCount":2}`.

## Share a value across tasks

Use `export.as` to update `$context`. Merge the new value with the existing context
when earlier context entries must remain accessible. Use `$workflow.input` to read
values supplied when the workflow started.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: share-order-context
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - identifyCustomer:
      set:
        customerId: ${ .customer.id }
      export:
        as: '${ $context + { customerId: .customerId } }'
  - prepareOrder:
      set:
        orderId: ${ $workflow.input.orderId }
        customerId: ${ $context.customerId }
```

Save it as `share-order-context.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f share-order-context.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples share-order-context --input '{"orderId":"ORD-803","customer":{"id":"C-100"}}'
```

The second task reads the customer from `$context` and the order ID from `$workflow.input`: expect
`{"orderId":"ORD-803","customerId":"C-100"}`.

See [Data Flow](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl.md#data-flow) for validation order and expression scopes.



# How to use input, output, and export

This guide explains how to work with data flow in Lemline workflows, focusing on input validation, output transformation, and exporting data to the global context. You'll learn how to control data as it flows through your workflow.

## Understanding Data Flow in Lemline

Lemline's data flow model consists of three main components:

1. Input: Data coming into a task, including validation and transformation

2. Output: Data produced by a task, including transformation and validation

3. Export: Data promoted to the global workflow context for use across the workflow

Understanding how to use these components effectively is key to building robust workflows.

## Run the Examples

Each example below is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html) and keep its worker
running. Run the commands from a second terminal in the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute
`java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`. The worker logs `Workflow completed with output` with each result. The
examples that call HTTP services use the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop);
start it from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

## Working with Workflow Input

### Defining Workflow Input Schema

You can define an input schema at the workflow level to validate incoming data:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: io-input-schema
  version: '1.0.0'
  title: Order Processing Workflow
input:
  schema:
    document:
      type: object
      required:
        - orderId
        - customerId
        - items
      properties:
        orderId:
          type: string
          pattern: ^ORD-[0-9]{6}$
        customerId:
          type: string
        items:
          type: array
          minItems: 1
          items:
            type: object
            required:
              - productId
              - quantity
            properties:
              productId:
                type: string
              quantity:
                type: integer
                minimum: 1
do:
  - acceptOrder:
      set:
        accepted: ${ .orderId }
```

Save it as `defining-workflow-input-schema.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f defining-workflow-input-schema.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples io-input-schema --input '{"orderId":"ORD-000123","customerId":"C-100","items":[{"productId":"SKU-1","quantity":2}]}'
bin/lemline instance start examples io-input-schema --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1","customerId":"C-100","items":[{"productId":"SKU-1","quantity":2}]}'
```

The first instance completes with `{"accepted":"ORD-000123"}`. The second is refused before any instance exists: the CLI prints `Input validation failed against workflow schema`, because `ORD-1` does not match the pattern.

This schema ensures that workflow input contains the required fields with the correct data types and formats.

### Accessing Workflow Input

You can access the original workflow input in any task using `$workflow.input`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: accessing-workflow-input
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - summarize:
      set:
        itemCount: ${ .items | length }
  - processOrder:
      set:
        orderId: ${ $workflow.input.orderId }
        customerId: ${ $workflow.input.customerId }
        itemCount: ${ .itemCount }
```

Save it as `accessing-workflow-input.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f accessing-workflow-input.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples accessing-workflow-input --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1","customerId":"C-100","items":[{"productId":"SKU-1"},{"productId":"SKU-2"}]}'
```

The second task only receives `{"itemCount":2}` from the first, but reads the IDs from `$workflow.input`: expect `{"orderId":"ORD-1","customerId":"C-100","itemCount":2}`.

### Default Input Values

You can provide default values for workflow input fields:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: default-workflow-input
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  from: '${ { priority: "NORMAL", currency: "USD" } + . }'
do:
  - recordOrder:
      set:
        orderId: ${ .orderId }
        priority: ${ .priority }
        currency: ${ .currency }
```

Save it as `default-workflow-input.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f default-workflow-input.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples default-workflow-input --input '{"orderId":"ORD-2"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples default-workflow-input --input '{"orderId":"ORD-3","currency":"EUR"}'
```

Expect `{"orderId":"ORD-2","priority":"NORMAL","currency":"USD"}`, then `{"orderId":"ORD-3","priority":"NORMAL","currency":"EUR"}`.
The workflow-level `input.from` expression merges defaults with the input before the first task runs. Values supplied by the caller take precedence. `$workflow.input` still holds the input as the caller supplied it.

## Task Input Processing

### Implicit Input

By default, each task receives the output of the previous task as its input:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: implicit-input
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - taskA:
      set:
        value: 42
        message: Hello
  - taskB:
      set:
        originalValue: ${ .value }
        newMessage: ${ .message + ", World!" }
```

Save it as `implicit-input.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f implicit-input.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples implicit-input
```

Expect `{"originalValue":42,"newMessage":"Hello, World!"}`.

### Input Transformation

You can transform the input data before task execution:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: input-transformation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - formatData:
      input:
        from:
          user: ${ .userProfile }
          contactInfo:
            email: ${ .userProfile.email | ascii_downcase }
            phone: ${ .userProfile.phone | gsub("[^0-9]"; "") }
      set:
        formattedUser:
          id: ${ .user.id }
          name: ${ .user.name }
          email: ${ .contactInfo.email }
          phone: ${ .contactInfo.phone }
```

Save it as `input-transformation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f input-transformation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples input-transformation --input '{"userProfile":{"id":"C-100","name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"Ada@Example.com","phone":"+44 (20) 7946-0000"}}'
```

Expect `{"formattedUser":{"id":"C-100","name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com","phone":"442079460000"}}`.

The `input.from` field lets you reshape the incoming data before it's used in the task.

### Input Schema Validation

You can validate task input against a schema:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: input-schema-validation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - ValidatePaymentInfo:
      set:
        validPayment: true
        formattedAmount: '${ "$" + (.amount | tostring) }'
      input:
        schema:
          document:
            type: object
            required:
              - amount
              - currency
              - paymentMethod
            properties:
              amount:
                type: number
                minimum: 0.01
              currency:
                type: string
                enum:
                  - USD
                  - EUR
                  - GBP
              paymentMethod:
                type: object
                required:
                  - type
                properties:
                  type:
                    type: string
                    enum:
                      - CREDIT
                      - DEBIT
                      - PAYPAL
```

Save it as `input-schema-validation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f input-schema-validation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples input-schema-validation --input '{"amount":25,"currency":"EUR","paymentMethod":{"type":"CREDIT"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples input-schema-validation --input '{"amount":25,"currency":"JPY","paymentMethod":{"type":"CREDIT"}}'
```

The first instance completes with `{"validPayment":true,"formattedAmount":"$25"}`. The second faults at the task with a `validation` error, because `JPY` is not one of the allowed currencies.

If the input doesn't match the schema, a validation error is raised.

## Task Output Processing

### Basic Output

The output of a `set` task is the object defined under `set`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: basic-output
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - generateOutput:
      set:
        status: SUCCESS
        result: 42
```

Save it as `basic-output.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f basic-output.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples basic-output
```

Expect `{"status":"SUCCESS","result":42}`.

This task produces an output object with `status`, `result`, and `timestamp` fields.

### Output Transformation

You can transform the output data before passing it to the next task:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: output-transformation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - getCustomer:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/" + .customerId }
      output:
        as:
          customer: ${ .name }
          tier: ${ .tier }
          isGold: ${ .tier == "gold" }
```

Save it as `output-transformation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f output-transformation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples output-transformation --input '{"customerId":"C-100"}'
```

The shop returns the whole customer; `output.as` keeps three fields: `{"customer":"Ada Lovelace","tier":"gold","isGold":true}`.

The `output.as` field reshapes the task result before it's passed to the next task.

### Output Schema Validation

You can validate task output against a schema:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: output-schema-validation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - GenerateUserProfile:
      set:
        profile:
          id: ${ .userId }
          name: ${ .firstName + " " + .lastName }
          email: ${ .emailAddress }
          memberSince: ${ .joinDate }
      output:
        schema:
          document:
            type: object
            required:
              - profile
            properties:
              profile:
                type: object
                required:
                  - id
                  - name
                  - email
                properties:
                  id:
                    type: string
                  name:
                    type: string
                  email:
                    type: string
                    format: email
```

Save it as `output-schema-validation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f output-schema-validation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples output-schema-validation --input '{"userId":"C-100","firstName":"Ada","lastName":"Lovelace","emailAddress":"ada@example.com","joinDate":"2020-01-01"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples output-schema-validation --input '{"userId":"C-100","firstName":"Ada","lastName":"Lovelace","joinDate":"2020-01-01"}'
```

The first instance returns the profile. In the second, `email` is `null`, which is not a string: the task faults with a `validation` error.

If the output doesn't match the schema, a validation error is raised.

## Exporting Data to Global Context

### Basic Export

The `export` field lets you promote data to the global workflow context:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: basic-export
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchCustomerData:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/" + .customerId }
      export:
        as:
          customer: ${ . }
  - greetCustomer:
      set:
        greeting: ${ "Hello " + $context.customer.name }
```

Save it as `basic-export.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f basic-export.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples basic-export --input '{"customerId":"C-100"}'
```

The second task reads the exported customer: expect `{"greeting":"Hello Ada Lovelace"}`.

Later tasks can read the exported customer data from `$context.customer`.

### Exporting Selected Fields

You can export specific fields rather than the entire output:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: exporting-selected-fields
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - getProduct:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/" + .productId }
      export:
        as:
          productName: ${ .name }
          unitPrice: ${ .price }
  - showContext:
      set:
        context: ${ $context }
```

Save it as `exporting-selected-fields.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f exporting-selected-fields.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples exporting-selected-fields --input '{"productId":"SKU-2"}'
```

The last task shows the context: `{"context":{"productName":"Watering can","unitPrice":12}}`.

This exports only the selected fields to the global context.

### Export with Transformation

You can transform data during export:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: export-with-transformation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchProductData:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/products
        query:
          size: '10'
      export:
        as:
          products: ${ .items }
          productMap: '${ .items | map({key: .id, value: .name}) | from_entries }'
          categories: ${ .items | map(.category) | unique }
  - showContext:
      set:
        context: ${ $context }
```

Save it as `export-with-transformation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f export-with-transformation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples export-with-transformation
```

The context holds the seven products, a `productMap` from ID to name, and `categories`: `["clothing","garden","home"]`.

This exports the original products array plus derived data structures.

### Export Schema Validation

You can validate exported data against a schema:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: io-export-schema-validation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - validateExportedData:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/" + .productId }
      export:
        as:
          validatedProduct: ${ . }
        schema:
          document:
            type: object
            required:
              - validatedProduct
            properties:
              validatedProduct:
                type: object
                required:
                  - id
                  - name
                  - category
                properties:
                  id:
                    type: string
                  name:
                    type: string
                  category:
                    type: string
                    enum:
                      - garden
                      - home
  - showContext:
      set:
        context: ${ $context }
```

Save it as `export-schema-validation.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f export-schema-validation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples io-export-schema-validation --input '{"productId":"SKU-1"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples io-export-schema-validation --input '{"productId":"SKU-6"}'
```

SKU-1 is a garden product: the context holds it. SKU-6 is clothing, which the schema does not allow: the task faults with a `validation` error.

This ensures the exported data meets the specified schema requirements.

## Comprehensive Example: Order Processing

This workflow validates the input, routes the order based on its total, and
returns the order ID and processing status.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: validate-and-route-order
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  schema:
    format: json
    document:
      type: object
      required: [orderId, total]
      properties:
        orderId:
          type: string
        total:
          type: number
          minimum: 0
do:
  - routeOrder:
      switch:
        - largeOrder:
            when: ${ .total >= 1000 }
            then: requestReview
        - automatic:
            then: acceptOrder
  - requestReview:
      set:
        status: needs-review
      then: exit
  - acceptOrder:
      set:
        status: accepted
output:
  as: '${ { orderId: $workflow.input.orderId, status: .status } }'
```

Save it as `validate-and-route-order.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f validate-and-route-order.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples validate-and-route-order --input '{"orderId":"ORD-301","total":250}'
bin/lemline instance start examples validate-and-route-order --input '{"orderId":"ORD-302","total":1500}'
```

Expect `{"orderId":"ORD-301","status":"accepted"}` and `{"orderId":"ORD-302","status":"needs-review"}`.

## Advanced Patterns

### Chain of Responsibility

Chain multiple data transformations for complex processing:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: chain-of-responsibility
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - step1:
      set:
        intermediateResult: ${ .rawData | fromjson }
  - step2:
      set:
        processedData: ${ .intermediateResult | map(.value) }
  - step3:
      set:
        finalResult: ${ .processedData | add }
      export:
        as:
          result: ${ .finalResult }
  - showContext:
      set:
        context: ${ $context }
```

Save it as `chain-of-responsibility.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f chain-of-responsibility.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples chain-of-responsibility --input '{"rawData":"[{\"value\":1},{\"value\":2},{\"value\":3}]"}'
```

Expect `{"context":{"result":6}}`.

### Selective Processing with Condition-Based Export

Export different data based on conditions:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: selective-processing-with-condition-based-export
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - conditionalExport:
      set:
        status: '${ if .code == 200 then "SUCCESS" else "ERROR" end }'
        successData: ${ if .code == 200 then .data else null end }
        errorData: ${ if .code != 200 then .error else null end }
      export:
        as:
          result: '${ if .status == "SUCCESS" then .successData else .errorData end }'
          isError: ${ .status == "ERROR" }
  - showContext:
      set:
        context: ${ $context }
```

Save it as `selective-processing-with-condition-based-export.yaml`:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f selective-processing-with-condition-based-export.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples selective-processing-with-condition-based-export --input '{"code":200,"data":{"orderId":"ORD-1"}}'
```
