```BASH
bin/lemline instance start examples declaration
bin/lemline definition post -f http-secrets-reference.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-secrets-reference
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `declaration` |`{"tokenSet":true,"user":"demo"}` |
| `http-secrets-reference` |The partner stock with `"authenticatedWith":"bearer"` |

Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```



# HTTP Protocol Reference

This reference describes how Lemline executes `call: http` tasks: which arguments are supported, how requests are built, and what the task returns.

## HTTP Support Overview

| Feature |Support |
--------------------
| Methods |Any HTTP method (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, ...) |
| URL |Plain URL or runtime expression |
| Headers and query parameters |Map of values or a runtime expression returning an object |
| Request body |JSON, sent for `post`, `put` and `patch` |
| Authentication |`basic` and `bearer` (inline or via `use.authentications`) |
| Output |`content` (default), `response` or `raw` |
| Redirects |`redirect: true` follows redirects |

Not supported: URI template placeholders, connection definitions, form or multipart bodies, OAuth 2.0 and other authentication schemes, per-call timeouts, proxies, cookies, HTTP-level circuit breakers, and runner settings to tune the HTTP client.

## Basic HTTP Request

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: basic-http-request
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchCustomer:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/C-100
```

## URL Construction

### Plain URL

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-literal-endpoint
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/C-100
```

### Runtime Expression

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-expression-endpoint
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/" + .customer.id }
```

The expression must return a string. RFC 6570 placeholders such as `{userId}` are not expanded: build dynamic URLs with an expression.

## Request Headers

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-request-headers
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
        headers:
          Accept: application/json
          X-Request-Id: ${ .requestId }
```

`headers` can also be a single runtime expression that returns an object. Every value is sent as a string.

## Query Parameters

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-query-parameters
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/products
        query:
          page: "1"
          category: ${ .category }
```

Query parameters are appended to the URL. Like `headers`, `query` can be a runtime expression returning an object.

## Request Body

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: request-body
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - createCustomer:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers
        body:
          name: ${ .name }
          email: ${ .email }
```

The body is serialized as JSON and sent with `Content-Type: application/json`. It is only sent for `post`, `put` and `patch`.

## Response Handling

### Output Formats

| `output` |Task result |
-------------------------
| `content` (default) |The response body: parsed JSON when the response content type contains `json`, a string when it contains `text`, otherwise the body encoded in Base64 |
| `response` |An object with `request` (`method`, `uri`, `headers`), `statusCode`, `headers` and `content` |
| `raw` |The response body encoded in Base64 |

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: output-formats
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchProducts:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/products
        output: response
      output:
        as: '${ { status: .statusCode, ids: [.content.items[].id] } }'
```

### Error Status Handling

A response whose status is not 2xx makes the task fail with a `communication` error. Its `status` is the HTTP status and its title contains the status code and the response body (for example `HTTP 404: ...`). A call that gets no response (unknown host, refused connection, timeout) also fails with a `communication` error, with status 500 and a title naming the server (for example `Unable to reach https://api.example.com: unresolved host`). Catch them with `try`, and add `status` to the filter to handle one status only:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: error-status-handling
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchData:
      try:
        - callApi:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/" + .productId }
      catch:
        errors:
          with:
            type: https://open-workflow-specification.org/spec/1.0.0/errors/communication
        as: apiError
        do:
          - fallback:
              set:
                data: []
                reason: ${ $apiError.title }
```

## Authentication

Authentication fields evaluate runtime expressions, so they can read secrets. A workflow only sees the secrets it declares in `use.secrets`; an undeclared secret evaluates to `null` and the task faults.

### Basic Authentication

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-inline-basic-authentication
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  secrets:
    - API_USER
    - API_PASSWORD
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint:
          uri: http://127.0.0.1:8787/partner/stock
          authentication:
            basic:
              username: ${ $secrets.API_USER }
              password: ${ $secrets.API_PASSWORD }
```

### Bearer Token

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-inline-bearer-token
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  secrets:
    - API_TOKEN
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint:
          uri: http://127.0.0.1:8787/partner/stock
          authentication:
            bearer:
              token: ${ $secrets.API_TOKEN }
```

### Named Authentication

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: named-authentication
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  secrets:
    - API_TOKEN
  authentications:
    apiAuth:
      bearer:
        token: ${ $secrets.API_TOKEN }
do:
  - callApi:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint:
          uri: http://127.0.0.1:8787/partner/stock
          authentication:
            use: apiAuth
```

An API key can be sent as a regular header. OAuth 2.0 is not supported yet: a task using it fails with a `runtime` error titled `Unsupported OAuth2 authentication`.

## Redirects

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-follow-redirects
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/old-stock
        redirect: true
```

Without `redirect: true`, a redirect response (3xx) is not followed and fails the task like any other non-2xx status, as in the example below.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: http-no-redirect
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetch:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/old-stock
```

## Timeouts

The runner's HTTP client uses fixed limits: 15 seconds to connect, 30 seconds for the whole request and 30 seconds of socket inactivity. They cannot be changed, and a task-level `timeout` is not applied to HTTP calls.

## Retry Behavior

HTTP calls are not retried automatically. Use `try` with `retry`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: retry-behavior
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - fetchData:
      try:
        - callApi:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              query:
                fail: '503'
                failTimes: ${ .failures // 0 | tostring }
                key: ${ $workflow.id }
      catch:
        errors:
          with:
            type: https://open-workflow-specification.org/spec/1.0.0/errors/communication
        retry:
          delay:
            seconds: 2
          backoff:
            exponential: {}
          limit:
            attempt:
              count: 5
```

## HTTP Request Examples

### JSON POST Request

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: json-post-request
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - createReservation:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/reservations
        headers:
          Idempotency-Key: ${ .orderId }
        body:
          orderId: ${ .orderId }
          items: ${ .items }
        output: response
```

### GraphQL Query

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: customer-graphql-lookup
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - queryGraphQL:
      call: http
      with:
        method: post
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/graphql
        body:
          query: "query($id: ID!) { customer(id: $id) { name email } }"
          variables:
            id: ${ .customerId }
```

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow that calls the
[tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop). Complete
[the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and start the shop
from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH

```

The authentication examples read the shop's demo credentials from secrets. Stop the setup worker with Ctrl+C, export
them, and start the worker again (with the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`):

```BASH

export API_PASSWORD='demo-password'
export API_TOKEN='demo-token'
bin/lemline listen --debug
```

From a second terminal in the setup directory, register and start each example:

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f basic-http-request.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples basic-http-request
bin/lemline definition post -f http-literal-endpoint.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-literal-endpoint
bin/lemline definition post -f http-expression-endpoint.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-expression-endpoint --input '{"customer":{"id":"C-200"}}'
bin/lemline definition post -f http-request-headers.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-request-headers --input '{"requestId":"REQ-42"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f http-query-parameters.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-query-parameters --input '{"category":"home"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f request-body.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples request-body --input '{"name":"Hedy Lamarr","email":"hedy@example.com"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f output-formats.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples output-formats
bin/lemline definition post -f error-status-handling.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples error-status-handling --input '{"productId":"SKU-404"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f http-inline-basic-authentication.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-inline-basic-authentication
bin/lemline definition post -f http-inline-bearer-token.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-inline-bearer-token
bin/lemline definition post -f named-authentication.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples named-authentication
bin/lemline definition post -f http-follow-redirects.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-follow-redirects
bin/lemline definition post -f http-no-redirect.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples http-no-redirect
bin/lemline definition post -f retry-behavior.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples retry-behavior --input '{"failures":2}'
bin/lemline definition post -f json-post-request.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples json-post-request --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1601","items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":1}]}'
bin/lemline definition post -f graphql-query.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples customer-graphql-lookup --input '{"customerId":"C-100"}'
```

| Example |Expected result |

| `basic-http-request`, `http-literal-endpoint` |Customer C-100, Ada Lovelace |
| `http-expression-endpoint` |Customer C-200, Alan Turing |
| `http-request-headers` |The stock; the shop's request list shows `x-request-id: REQ-42` |
| `http-query-parameters` |The home products, SKU-4 and SKU-5 |
| `request-body` |The new customer `C-901` |
| `output-formats` |`{"status":200,"ids":["SKU-1","SKU-2","SKU-3"]}` |
| `error-status-handling` |`{"data":[],"reason":"HTTP 404: …"}` |
| `http-inline-basic-authentication` |The partner stock with `"authenticatedWith":"basic"` |
| `http-inline-bearer-token`, `named-authentication` |The partner stock with `"authenticatedWith":"bearer"` |
| `http-follow-redirects` |The stock, read from `/stock` after the 301 |
| `http-no-redirect` |Faults with a `communication` error, status 301 |
| `retry-behavior` |The stock after two retries |
| `json-post-request` |The full response, `statusCode` 200 with the reservation in `content` |
| `customer-graphql-lookup` |`{"data":{"customer":{…"name":"Ada Lovelace"…}}}` |

# gRPC Protocol Reference

This page describes the support of `call: grpc` tasks in Lemline.

## gRPC Support Status

Lemline does not execute `call: grpc` tasks yet. The Open Workflow DSL defines them (see [gRPC calls](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#grpc-call)), and Lemline parses workflows that contain them, but no runner can run such a task: do not use it in workflows you deploy.

There are no `lemline.grpc.*` runner settings.

## Alternative

Expose the service over HTTP (for example with a gRPC-JSON transcoding proxy) and call it with `call: http`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: grpc-alternative
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - getStock:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: '${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/products/\(.sku | @uri)" }'
```

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f alternative.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples grpc-alternative --input '{"sku":"SKU-1"}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `grpc-alternative` |The garden hose with its stock |

Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

* [Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html)



# OpenAPI Reference

This page describes the support of `call: openapi` tasks in Lemline.

## OpenAPI Support Status

Lemline does not execute `call: openapi` tasks yet. The Open Workflow DSL defines them (see [OpenAPI calls](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#openapi-call)), and Lemline parses workflows that contain them, but no runner can run such a task: do not use it in workflows you deploy.

There are no `lemline.openapi.*` runner settings.

## Alternative

Call the operation's URL directly with `call: http`, using the method, path, query parameters and body described in the OpenAPI document:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: openapi-alternative
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - findGardenProducts:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/products
        query:
          category: garden
        output: content
```

```BASH

```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH

```

| `openapi-alternative` |The first page of garden products, SKU-1 to SKU-3 |

# AsyncAPI Reference

This page describes the support of `call: asyncapi` tasks in Lemline.

## AsyncAPI Support Status

Lemline does not execute `call: asyncapi` tasks yet. The Open Workflow DSL defines them (see [AsyncAPI calls](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#asyncapi-call)), and Lemline parses workflows that contain them, but no runner can run such a task: do not use it in workflows you deploy.

There are no `lemline.asyncapi.*` runner settings.

## Alternative

Exchange messages as CloudEvents with `emit` and `listen` tasks. They travel on the broker Lemline is configured with (see [Message Brokers](lemline-howto-brokers.html)):

```YAML
document:
  dsl: 1.0.3
  namespace: examples
  name: asyncapi-alternative
  version: 1.0.0
do:
  - publishOrder:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: com.example.order.created
            source: https://events.example.com/order-service
            data: ${ .order }
  - waitForPayment:
      listen:
        to:
          one:
            with:
              type: com.example.payment.received
```

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

The event examples need the tutorial publisher. Save it as `tutorial-publisher.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: tutorial-publisher
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - publish:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: ${ .type }
            source: https://events.example.com/tutorial
            data: ${ .data }
```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f tutorial-publisher.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f alternative.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples asyncapi-alternative --input '{"order":{"orderId":"ORD-1701"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.payment.received","data":{"orderId":"ORD-1701"}}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `asyncapi-alternative` |Emits `com.example.order.created`, waits, then completes with `[{"orderId":"ORD-1701"}]` after the payment event |

## Related Resources

* [HTTP Protocol Reference](lemline-ref-http.html)

* [Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html)



# Connections Reference

This reference explains how workflows reuse endpoint settings in Lemline.

## Connections Overview

Lemline has no "connection" object: there is no `use.connections` section, no connection pools to configure, no connection health checks, failover or circuit breakers, and no `lemline.connections.*` runner settings.

Workflows reuse settings with the reusable components of the Open Workflow DSL that Lemline supports in the `use` section:

| `use` section |Reused in |
----------------------------
| `authentications` |`call: http` endpoints (`authentication.use`) |
| `secrets` |Expressions, through `$secrets` |
| `functions` |`call: <function name>` |
| `errors` |`raise` tasks (`error: <name>`) |
| `retries` |`try` / `catch` (`retry: <name>`) |

## Reusing an Endpoint's Authentication

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: reusing-an-endpoint-s-authentication
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  secrets:
    - USER_API_TOKEN
  authentications:
    userApi:
      bearer:
        token: ${ $secrets.USER_API_TOKEN }
do:
  - getUser:
      call: http
      with:
        method: get
        endpoint:
          uri: http://127.0.0.1:8787/partner/stock
          authentication:
            use: userApi
```

## Reusing a Call with a Function

Wrap a call in a function and call it by name. The `with` values of the calling task are the function's input:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: reusing-a-call-with-a-function
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  functions:
    getCustomer:
      do:
        - request:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: ${ "http://127.0.0.1:8787/customers/" + .customerId }
do:
  - fetchCustomer:
      call: getCustomer
      with:
        customerId: ${ .id }
```

## Reusing a Retry Policy

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: reusing-a-retry-policy
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  retries:
    standard:
      delay:
        seconds: 2
      backoff:
        exponential: {}
      limit:
        attempt:
          count: 5
do:
  - fetchData:
      try:
        - callApi:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              query:
                fail: '503'
                failTimes: ${ .failures // 0 | tostring }
                key: ${ $workflow.id }
      catch:
        retry: standard
```

## Broker and Database Connections

The runner's own connections to the message broker and the database are set in the runner configuration, not in workflows. See [Runner Configuration Reference](lemline-ref-config.html) and [Message Brokers](lemline-howto-brokers.html).

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

The examples read secrets from the worker's environment. Stop the setup worker with Ctrl+C, export the values, and start it again:

```BASH
export USER_API_TOKEN='demo-token'
bin/lemline listen --debug
```

Run the next commands from a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f reusing-an-endpoint-s-authentication.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples reusing-an-endpoint-s-authentication
bin/lemline definition post -f reusing-a-call-with-a-function.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples reusing-a-call-with-a-function --input '{"id":"C-200"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f reusing-a-retry-policy.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples reusing-a-retry-policy --input '{"failures":1}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `reusing-an-endpoint-s-authentication` |The partner stock with `"authenticatedWith":"bearer"` |
| `reusing-a-call-with-a-function` |Customer C-200, Alan Turing |
| `reusing-a-retry-policy` |The stock after one retry |

Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```

# Serialization Reference

This reference describes the data formats Lemline reads and writes. None of them is configurable: there are no `lemline.serialization.*` or schema-registry settings.

## Serialization Overview

| What |Format |
----------------
| Workflow definitions |YAML or JSON |
| Workflow data (input, output, task results, context) |JSON values |
| Messages between runners (commands and events) |Protocol Buffers, binary on the broker |
| Workflow state stored in the database |Protocol Buffers as JSON (ProtoJSON) |
| Events emitted and received by workflows |CloudEvents in JSON |
| HTTP request bodies |JSON |
| JSON Schemas (`input.schema`, `output.schema`, `export.schema`) |JSON Schema draft 2020-12, written in JSON or YAML |

XML, Avro, CBOR and MessagePack are not supported, and there is no schema registry integration.

## Workflow Data

Workflow data is always a JSON value: object, array, string, number, boolean or `null`. Expressions (jq) read and produce JSON values.

* Numbers keep their decimal precision.

* Dates and times are strings; Lemline does not convert them to another type.

* Binary data is represented as a Base64 string, for example the body of an HTTP response returned with `output: raw`.

## HTTP Content Types

For `call: http` tasks:

* The request body is sent as JSON with `Content-Type: application/json`, for `post`, `put` and `patch` only.

* With `output: content` (the default), a response whose content type contains `json` is parsed as JSON, one that contains `text` becomes a string, and anything else becomes a Base64 string.

See [HTTP Protocol Reference](lemline-ref-http.html).

## Messaging

Runners exchange workflow commands and events as Protocol Buffers messages carrying the serialized workflow state, so any runner can continue any instance. The format is internal to Lemline: only Lemline runners and the gateway read these destinations.

CloudEvents emitted by `emit` tasks and consumed by `listen` tasks use the JSON format of the CloudEvents specification.

## Schema Validation

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: customer-input-schema
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  schema:
    format: json
    document:
      type: object
      required: [customerId]
      properties:
        customerId:
          type: string
do:
  - example:
      set:
        ready: true
```

Data that does not match its schema raises a `validation` error. External schemas referenced by URL are fetched at validation time.

## Error Handling

| Situation |Result |
---------------------
| Invalid workflow definition |`lemline definition post` rejects the file |
| Data does not match a schema |`validation` error |
| An expression fails |`expression` error |
| A message cannot be decoded by a runner |The message goes to the dead-letter destination of its source |

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f customer-input-schema.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples customer-input-schema --input '{"customerId":"C-100"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples customer-input-schema --input '{"customerId":100}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `{"customerId":"C-100"}` |Completes with `{"ready":true}` |
| `{"customerId":100}` |Refused by `instance start`: `integer found, string expected` |

## Related Resources

* [HTTP Protocol Reference](lemline-ref-http.html)

* [Message Brokers](lemline-howto-brokers.html)

* [Data Flow](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl.md#data-flow)



# Why Event-Driven Orchestration Beats the Database

This explanation explores the architectural advantages of Lemline's event-driven orchestration approach compared to traditional database-centric workflow engines. We'll examine the problems with conventional state persistence, explain event-driven principles, and analyze the performance implications.

## The Problem with Traditional State Persistence

Traditional workflow engines share a common architectural pattern: they rely heavily on a central database to store workflow state. While this approach seems logical at first glance, it introduces significant challenges:

### Database Transaction Overhead

Every workflow step in traditional engines typically requires multiple database transactions:

1. Read state: Retrieve the current workflow state from the database

2. Lock state: Acquire locks to prevent concurrent modifications

3. Execute logic: Perform the actual business logic

4. Update state: Save the updated workflow state

5. Update history: Record execution history and audit trail

6. Release locks: Free resources for other transactions

This pattern creates several issues:

* Transaction Volume: Even simple workflows generate high transaction volumes

* Lock Contention: Concurrent workflows compete for the same database resources

* Transaction Duration: Long-running tasks hold database connections and locks

* Write Amplification: Each logical step requires multiple physical writes

### Performance Bottlenecks

The database quickly becomes the performance bottleneck:

* I/O Limitations: Database performance is ultimately constrained by disk I/O

* Connection Pools: Limited connection pools restrict throughput

* Scaling Challenges: Vertical scaling becomes necessary, which is expensive and has limits

* Backup and Recovery: Larger databases take longer to backup and restore

* Index Maintenance: Indexes needed for performance consume additional resources

A medium-sized workflow system can easily generate millions of database operations per day, even with modest workflow volumes.

### High Infrastructure Costs

The infrastructure requirements grow rapidly:

* Expensive Storage: Need for high-performance SSD storage

* Memory Requirements: Large buffer pools for acceptable performance

* CPU Overhead: Transaction processing consumes substantial CPU resources

* Backup Storage: Large databases require significant backup capacity

* High Availability: Replication and failover systems add more complexity

### Reliability Challenges

Centralizing all state in a database introduces single points of failure:

* Database Availability: If the database is down, all workflow processing stops

* Complex Recovery: Recovering from database failures is non-trivial

* Transaction Boundaries: Determining proper transaction boundaries is challenging

* Partial Failures: Handling failures mid-transaction requires complex compensation logic

* Data Consistency: Maintaining consistency across distributed systems is difficult

## Event-Driven State Management Principles

Lemline takes a fundamentally different approach by embracing event-driven architecture principles:

### Event Sourcing Foundation

Instead of storing the current state, Lemline applies event sourcing concepts:

* Events as Truth: The sequence of events becomes the source of truth

* Derived State: Current state is derived from the event sequence when needed

* Immutable History: Events are immutable facts about what happened

* Natural Audit Trail: Event history provides a built-in audit trail

This approach decouples state management from persistence concerns.

### Message-First Architecture

Rather than using the database as the primary communication medium, Lemline uses messaging:

* Event Communication: Components communicate through events

* Asynchronous Processing: Tasks can execute asynchronously

* Natural Parallelism: Independent operations run in parallel automatically

* Loose Coupling: Components don't need direct knowledge of each other

This messaging foundation enables a more resilient and scalable system.

### Selective Persistence Strategy

Lemline only persists state when absolutely necessary:

* Wait States: Persistent storage for time-based operations

* Event Correlation: Storage for matching related events

* Long-Running Operations: Persistence for operations spanning days or weeks

* Outbox Pattern: Reliable message delivery with transactional guarantees

For many workflow types, most execution can happen without touching a database at all.

## The Architecture Advantages

### Minimal Database Interaction

In a traditional system, a 10-step workflow might require 30+ database operations. In Lemline, the same workflow might need only 2-3 database operations, or none at all for short-lived workflows.

Consider this comparison for a payment processing workflow:

| Workflow Step |Traditional Engine |Lemline |
----------------------------------------------
| Receive order |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Validate order |2 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Check inventory |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Process payment |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Generate invoice |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Wait for shipping |3 DB operations |1 DB operation |
| Send confirmation |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Complete order |3 DB operations |0 DB operations |
| Total |23 DB operations |1 DB operation |

This dramatic reduction in database operations translates directly to higher throughput, lower latency, and reduced infrastructure costs.

### Horizontal Scalability

Event-driven architectures enable true horizontal scalability:

* Stateless Processing: Most processing can be stateless

* Partition-Based Scaling: Scale by adding more processing nodes

* Natural Load Distribution: Message brokers distribute load across nodes

* No Central Bottleneck: No single component limits overall throughput

* Independent Scaling: Scale individual components based on their specific needs

### Resilience to Failures

The event-driven approach provides superior resilience:

* Inherent Fault Isolation: Component failures don't bring down the entire system

* Message Replay: Events can be replayed from the broker if needed

* Reduced Failure Domain: Each component has a smaller failure domain

* Simpler Recovery: Recovery often means simply restarting a component

* Graceful Degradation: System can continue operating in degraded modes

### Lower Operational Costs

Operational costs are significantly reduced:

* Reduced Database Size: Much smaller database footprint

* Lower IOPS Requirements: Fewer database operations mean lower IOPS needs

* Cheaper Storage Options: Less demanding storage requirements

* Simplified Backup: Smaller databases are easier to backup and restore

* Lower Memory Needs: Less data needs to be cached in memory

## When Lemline Uses a Database (and Why)

While Lemline minimizes database usage, it still leverages databases for specific scenarios:

### Wait States and Timers

When a workflow needs to pause execution for a period of time:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: 1.0.3
  namespace: examples
  name: wait-states-and-timers
  version: 1.0.0
do:
  - waitForPaymentWindow:
      wait: PT10S
      then: checkPaymentStatus
  - checkPaymentStatus:
      set:
        windowClosed: true
```

This wait operation is stored in the database with:

* Workflow instance ID

* Current position

* Wake-up time

* Next task to execute

A dedicated outbox processor periodically checks for expired waits and resumes the workflow.

### Event Correlation

When workflows need to correlate incoming events:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: 1.0.3
  namespace: examples
  name: event-correlation
  version: 1.0.0
do:
  - waitForShipmentEvents:
      listen:
        to:
          one:
            with:
              type: com.example.shipment.updated
            correlate:
              orderId:
                from: ${ .orderId }
                expect: ${ $workflow.input.orderId }
      then: processShipmentUpdates
  - processShipmentUpdates:
      set:
        orderId: ${ .[0].orderId }
        status: ${ .[0].status }
```

The correlation criteria are stored in the database to match against incoming events.

### Outbox Pattern Implementation

For guaranteed message delivery, Lemline uses the outbox pattern:

1. Database transaction inserts the message into an outbox table

2. Dedicated processor reads from the outbox and publishes to the message broker

3. After successful publication, the message is marked as processed

This ensures exactly-once message delivery semantics with transactional guarantees.

### Storage Efficiency

When Lemline does use the database, it's designed for maximum efficiency:

* Minimal Schema: Tables contain only essential fields

* Optimized Indexes: Carefully designed indexes for common query patterns

* TTL Mechanisms: Automatic purging of completed entries

* Batch Processing: Processing multiple records in batches

* Connection Pooling: Efficient connection management

## Performance Implications

### Benchmark Comparisons

Benchmarks comparing Lemline to traditional workflow engines show significant performance advantages:

#### Throughput (workflows per second)

| Scenario |Traditional Engine |Lemline |Improvement |
------------------------------------------------------
| Simple workflows |100 |500+ |5x |
| Medium complexity |50 |200+ |4x |
| Complex workflows |20 |60+ |3x |

#### Latency (average workflow execution time)

| Scenario |Traditional Engine |Lemline |Improvement |
------------------------------------------------------
| Simple workflows |500ms |100ms |5x |
| Medium complexity |1000ms |300ms |3.3x |
| Complex workflows |2500ms |800ms |3.1x |

#### Resource Utilization (relative to traditional engine)

| Resource |Traditional Engine |Lemline |
-----------------------------------------
| Database IOPS |100% |10-20% |
| Database storage |100% |15-30% |
| Database connections |100% |20-40% |
| Memory usage |100% |60-80% |
| CPU usage |100% |70-90% |

### Real-World Performance Characteristics

In production environments, Lemline demonstrates these characteristics:

* Linear Scaling: Performance scales linearly with added nodes

* Low Latency: Consistently low latency even under high load

* Predictable Behavior: Performance remains stable and predictable

* Burst Handling: Can handle sudden spikes in traffic

* Resource Efficiency: Makes efficient use of available resources

## When to Choose Each Approach

While event-driven orchestration offers significant advantages, there are scenarios where database-centric approaches might still be appropriate:

### Choose Event-Driven Orchestration When:

* High-volume workflows: Processing thousands of workflows per minute

* Performance-sensitive scenarios: Low latency requirements

* Cost-sensitive deployments: Need to minimize infrastructure costs

* Horizontally scalable environments: Cloud-native or microservices architectures

* Resilience is critical: Need for high availability and fault tolerance

### Database-Centric May Still Make Sense When:

* Very low volume workflows: Just a few workflows per day

* Complex transactions: Need for ACID semantics across multiple operations

* Legacy integration: Tight integration with existing database-centric systems

* Simplified operations: When operational simplicity outweighs performance

## Implementation Considerations

When adopting event-driven orchestration, consider these implementation factors:

### Message Broker Selection

The message broker becomes a critical component:

* Reliability: Choose a broker with strong delivery guarantees

* Throughput: Ensure the broker can handle your expected message volume

* Latency: Consider message delivery latency requirements

* Partitioning: Efficient partitioning for scalability

* Management: Operational simplicity and monitoring capabilities

### Event Schema Design

Well-designed event schemas are essential:

* Versioning: Include schema versions for forwards/backwards compatibility

* Self-Contained: Events should contain all necessary context

* Correlation IDs: Include identifiers for tracing related events

* Timestamps: Include event creation time

* Explicit Types: Clearly identify event types

### Observability

With distributed processing, observability becomes critical:

* Distributed Tracing: Implement tracing across components

* Metrics Collection: Gather metrics from all parts of the system

* Centralized Logging: Aggregate logs for comprehensive visibility

* Correlation IDs: Use consistent correlation IDs for tracking

* Health Monitoring: Monitor the health of all components

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

The event examples need the tutorial publisher. Save it as `tutorial-publisher.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: tutorial-publisher
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - publish:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: ${ .type }
            source: https://events.example.com/tutorial
            data: ${ .data }
```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f tutorial-publisher.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f wait-states-and-timers.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples wait-states-and-timers
bin/lemline definition post -f event-correlation.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples event-correlation --input '{"orderId":"ORD-1801"}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.shipment.updated","data":{"orderId":"OTHER","status":"in-transit"}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.shipment.updated","data":{"orderId":"ORD-1801","status":"delivered"}}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `wait-states-and-timers` |`{"windowClosed":true}` 10 to 20 seconds later: the worker picks up timers every 10 seconds |
| `event-correlation` |Ignores the update for `OTHER`, then completes with `{"orderId":"ORD-1801","status":"delivered"}` |

## Conclusion

Lemline's event-driven orchestration offers a fundamentally different approach to workflow execution that overcomes many limitations of traditional database-centric engines. By minimizing database interactions, embracing event-driven principles, and selectively using persistence only when necessary, Lemline achieves superior performance, scalability, and resilience while reducing operational costs.

The key takeaways:

1. Database Overhead Matters: Traditional workflow engines generate excessive database load

2. Events as First-Class Citizens: Treating events as the primary communication mechanism enables better architectures

3. Selective Persistence: Only persist what's absolutely necessary

4. Significant Performance Gains: Event-driven orchestration delivers measurable performance improvements

5. Cost Reduction: Lower infrastructure requirements translate to cost savings

6. Improved Resilience: More resilient to component failures and better fault isolation

For most modern workflow scenarios, event-driven orchestration provides a superior approach that aligns well with cloud-native, microservices, and distributed system architectures.



# Understanding Workflow Execution

This document explains how Lemline executes workflows, from parsing the definition to completion.

## Starting and observing an instance through the gateway

An application can submit a start request to the gRPC gateway. The gateway records the accepted request in its outbox in the orchestration database. The outbox publishes a command to the broker for a runner to execute.

As the instance runs, the runner emits lifecycle events. Lifecycle Analytics consumes them and stores the history that the gateway reads. Acceptance and visibility are separate moments: a successful `StartInstance` reply gives you the instance ID, and gateway history reads can return `NOT_FOUND` until the first lifecycle events reach analytics. The outbox preserves the accepted request while its command awaits delivery.

Follow a request from acceptance to completion in the [gateway tutorial](lemline-tutorial-gateway.html).

## Execution Model Overview

Lemline implements a node-based execution model for Open Workflow DSL:

1. Parsing: The workflow definition (YAML/JSON) is parsed into a structured object model

2. Graph Construction: A directed graph of nodes is created from the model

3. State Management: Each node maintains its own execution state

4. Execution Flow: Nodes execute in sequence according to the workflow definition

5. Data Transformation: Data flows through the workflow, being transformed by expressions

## Workflow Lifecycle

### 1. Initialization Phase

When a workflow definition is submitted to Lemline:

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Parse YAML │ ─> │  Validate   │ ─> │ Construct   │ ─> │  Register   │
│  or JSON    │    │  Schema     │    │ Node Graph  │    │  Workflow   │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
```

1. Parsing: The YAML/JSON is parsed into a data structure

2. Schema Validation: The structure is validated against the Open Workflow schema

3. Node Graph Construction: A directed graph of `NodeInstance` objects is created

4. Registration: The workflow is registered in the Lemline registry

### 2. Instantiation Phase

When a workflow instance is created:

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Create     │ ─> │  Validate   │ ─> │  Initialize │ ─> │ Begin       │
│  Instance   │    │  Input      │    │  Context    │    │ Execution   │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
```

1. Instance Creation: A new `WorkflowInstance` is created

2. Input Validation: Input data is validated against the input schema

3. Context Initialization: Initial data context is created with the input data

4. Execution Start: The execution begins with the root node

### 3. Execution Phase

During workflow execution:

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Execute    │ ─> │  Evaluate   │ ─> │  Determine  │
│  Current    │    │  State &    │    │  Next       │ ─┐
│  Node       │    │  Expressions│    │  Node       │  │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘  │
       ▲                                                │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. Node Execution: The current node is executed

2. State Evaluation: The node's state is evaluated, and expressions are processed

3. Next Node Determination: The next node is determined based on the current state

4. Continuation: The process repeats until completion or suspension

### 4. Completion Phase

When workflow execution finishes:

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Validate   │ ─> │  Construct  │ ─> │  Update     │ ─> │  Emit       │
│  Output     │    │  Result     │    │  State      │    │  Events     │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
```

1. Output Validation: Final data is validated against the output schema

2. Result Construction: The workflow result is constructed

3. State Update: The workflow state is updated to "completed"

4. Event Emission: Completion events are emitted

## Node-Based Execution Model

Lemline's core execution model is based on a graph of nodes representing workflow tasks:

### Node Structure

Each node in the workflow graph has:

```KOTLIN
class NodeInstance<T : Task> {
    val node: T                      // The task definition
    val position: NodePosition       // Unique position identifier
    val parent: NodeInstance<*>?     // Parent node (if any)
    val children: List<NodeInstance<*>> // Child nodes
    
    var state: NodeState             // Current execution state
    
    fun execute(): NodeState         // Execute the node
}
```

### Node Position

Node positions uniquely identify nodes within a workflow:

```
/do/0/try/do/1
 │  │ │   │  │
 │  │ │   │  └─ Second task in the do block
 │  │ │   └──── Do block within try
 │  │ └──────── Try task
 │  └────────── First task in the main do block
 └───────────── Root of workflow
```

This hierarchical addressing enables:

* Precise error reporting

* State tracking at specific positions

* Resume capability at exact positions

### Node State

Each node maintains its own state:

```KOTLIN
data class NodeState(
    val status: NodeStatus,         // READY, RUNNING, COMPLETED, SUSPENDED, FAILED
    val input: JsonElement,         // Input data
    val output: JsonElement,        // Output data
    val variables: Map<String, JsonElement>, // Local variables
    val error: WorkflowError?       // Error information (if failed)
)
```

## Data Flow and Context Management

Data flows through the workflow in a structured way:

### Hierarchical Scoping

Variables follow hierarchical scoping rules:

```
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Root Scope                             │
│ └───────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ Task A Scope                     │ │
│  │ └───────────────────────────┐    │ │
│  │  │ Nested Task B Scope      │    │ │
│  │  │                          │    │ │
│  │  └───────────────────────────┘    │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

When resolving variables, Lemline searches:

1. The current node's scope

2. Parent scopes (up to the root)

### Expression Evaluation

JQ expressions are evaluated against the current context:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: expression-evaluation
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - setTax:
      set:
        taxAmount: "${ .orderTotal * .taxRate }"
```

The expression `.orderTotal * .taxRate` is evaluated with:

1. Current node's variables

2. Parent scope variables

3. Workflow input

### Data Transformation Flow

As data moves through the workflow:

```
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│  Input   │     │  Node A  │     │  Node B  │
│  Data    │ ──> │  Process │ ──> │  Process │ ──> ...
│          │     │          │     │          │
└──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘
```

Each node:

1. Receives input data

2. Processes and transforms it

3. Outputs result to next node

## Two-Phase Execution

Lemline implements a two-phase execution model:

### Synchronous Execution Phase

Control flow nodes execute synchronously:

* `do` - Sequential tasks

* `switch` - Conditional branching

* `for` - Iterations

* `fork` - Parallel execution

* `try` - Error handling

* `set` - Variable assignment

These nodes complete their execution immediately.

### Asynchronous Execution Phase

Activity nodes may execute asynchronously:

* `callHTTP` - External API calls

* `callOpenAPI/callGRPC` - Remote service calls

* `wait` - Time-based waiting

* `listen` - Event waiting

* `run` - External process execution

These nodes can pause workflow execution, creating a "suspension point."

## Suspension and Resumption

When a workflow encounters an asynchronous operation:

### Suspension Process

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Encounter  │ ─> │  Save       │ ─> │  Create     │ ─> │  Wait for   │
│  Async Node │    │  State      │    │  Outbox     │    │  Event      │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
```

1. Workflow execution reaches an asynchronous node

2. Current state is saved to the database

3. An outbox record is created for reliable processing

4. Execution suspends, waiting for completion event

### Resumption Process

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Receive    │ ─> │  Load       │ ─> │  Process    │ ─> │  Continue   │
│  Event      │    │  State      │    │  Result     │    │  Execution  │
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
```

1. A completion event is received

2. Workflow state is loaded from the database

3. Async operation result is processed

4. Execution continues from the suspension point

## Error Handling

Lemline provides robust error handling:

### Error Types

Errors are categorized by type:

* Configuration: Issues in the workflow definition

* Validation: Schema validation failures

* Expression: JQ expression evaluation errors

* Runtime: Errors during workflow execution

### Error Propagation

When an error occurs:

```
┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐
│ Error   │     │ Check   │     │ Parent  │
│ Occurs  │ ──> │ Current │ ──> │ Try     │ ──> ...
│         │     │ Try     │     │ Blocks  │
└─────────┘     └─────────┘     └─────────┘
```

1. Error information is captured

2. Current `try` block is checked for matching `catch`

3. If not caught, error propagates to parent `try` blocks

4. If never caught, workflow fails

### Retry Mechanism

When error is caught and retry is configured:

```
┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐
│ Error   │     │ Evaluate│     │ Wait    │     │ Retry   │
│ Caught  │ ──> │ Retry   │ ──> │ Backoff │ ──> │ Try     │
│         │     │ Policy  │     │ Period  │     │ Block   │
└─────────┘     └─────────┘     └─────────┘     └─────────┘
```

1. Retry policy is evaluated

2. If retry is allowed, a wait period is calculated

3. After the wait, the `try` block is re-executed

## Performance Considerations

The Lemline execution model is designed for:

### Efficiency

* Minimal State: Only essential state is persisted

* Lazy Evaluation: Expressions are evaluated only when needed

* Targeted Persistence: State is persisted only at suspension points

### Scalability

* Stateless Execution: Between suspension points, execution is stateless

* Horizontal Scaling: Multiple instances can process different workflows

* Microservices Alignment: Fits naturally into microservices architecture

### Reliability

* Outbox Pattern: Ensures reliable message delivery

* Atomic Operations: Database operations use transactions

* Idempotent Processing: Events can be safely processed multiple times

## Observability

The execution model provides comprehensive observability:

### Tracing

Each workflow execution generates a trace with:

* Node transitions

* Expression evaluations

* State changes

* Error occurrences

### Metrics

Key metrics include:

* Execution time per node

* Wait time at suspension points

* Error rates

* Retry counts

### Logging

Structured logging captures:

* Execution events

* Data transformations

* Error details

* External interactions

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH

bin/lemline instance start examples expression-evaluation --input '{"orderTotal":200,"taxRate":0.2}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `expression-evaluation` |`{"taxAmount":40}` |

# Open Workflow DSL in Lemline

Open Workflow is a declarative language for composing named tasks in YAML or JSON.
A workflow defines metadata, data contracts, and the tasks that act on the data.
Lemline implements the subset described in [Supported Features](lemline-ref-supported-features.html).

## Definitions and execution

A definition has a stable identity under `document`. Each execution carries its own
input and state. A workflow instance runs the tasks under `do` in order unless a task
provides a different flow directive.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: validate-and-route-order
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  schema:
    format: json
    document:
      type: object
      required: [orderId, total]
      properties:
        orderId:
          type: string
        total:
          type: number
          minimum: 0
do:
  - routeOrder:
      switch:
        - largeOrder:
            when: ${ .total >= 1000 }
            then: requestReview
        - automatic:
            then: acceptOrder
  - requestReview:
      set:
        status: needs-review
      then: exit
  - acceptOrder:
      set:
        status: accepted
output:
  as: '${ { orderId: $workflow.input.orderId, status: .status } }'
```

## Data and expressions

A task receives input as `.`. Use `${ ... }` to evaluate a jq expression. The original
input is available as `$workflow.input`. Tasks can share values through `$context` by
exporting them with `export.as`.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: transform-workflow-data
  version: '1.0.0'
input:
  from: '${ { customer: .user, items: .payload.items } }'
do:
  - summarize:
      set:
        customerId: ${ .customer.id }
        itemCount: ${ .items | length }
output:
  as: '${ { customerId, itemCount } }'
```

## Resource declarations

The `use` section defines shared resources. For example, a named retry policy can be
referenced from any compatible catch block.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: retry-and-fallback
  version: '1.0.0'
use:
  retries:
    transient:
      delay: PT2S
      backoff:
        exponential: {}
      limit:
        attempt:
          count: 3
do:
  - fetchInventory:
      try:
        - requestInventory:
            call: http
            with:
              method: get
              endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              query:
                fail: '503'
                failTimes: ${ .failures // 0 | tostring }
                key: ${ $workflow.id }
      catch:
        errors:
          with:
            type: https://open-workflow-specification.org/spec/1.0.0/errors/communication
            status: 503
        retry: transient
        do:
          - useCachedInventory:
              set:
                inventory: []
                stale: true
```

See [How to Define a Workflow](lemline-howto-define-workflow.html) for authoring steps.

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f validate-and-route-order.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples validate-and-route-order --input '{"orderId":"ORD-301","total":250}'
bin/lemline definition post -f transform-workflow-data.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples transform-workflow-data --input '{"user":{"id":"C-100"},"payload":{"items":[{"id":"SKU-1"}]}}'
bin/lemline definition post -f retry-and-fallback.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples retry-and-fallback --input '{"failures":5}'
```

| Example |Expected result |
----------------------------
| `validate-and-route-order` |`{"orderId":"ORD-301","status":"accepted"}` |
| `transform-workflow-data` |`{"customerId":"C-100","itemCount":1}` |
| `retry-and-fallback` |`{"inventory":[],"stale":true}` after four failed calls; allow about a minute |

Stop the shop when you are done:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml down
```



# Fan-out and fan-in

Fan-out distributes work. Fan-in brings the results together. The DSL has several
ways to model these patterns, depending on where the work happens.

## Run independent branches

A `fork` starts its branches concurrently. A non-competing fork joins their results
after all branches finish. Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) and supply `{"orderId":"QUOTE-1"}` to request the stock level and a shipping quote.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: parallel-order-checks
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - checkOrder:
      fork:
        branches:
          - checkStock:
              call: http
              with:
                method: get
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
              output:
                as: '${ { available: .available } }'
          - checkShipping:
              call: http
              with:
                method: post
                endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/express
                body: ${ . }
      output:
        as: '${ { checks: . } }'
```

## Iterate over input data

A `for` task runs its body for each item of a collection. Bind the current value with
`each` and its index with `at`.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: map-order-items
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - calculateTotals:
      for:
        each: item
        in: ${ .items }
        at: index
      do:
        - calculateLine:
            set:
              itemId: ${ $item.id }
              index: ${ $index }
              lineTotal: ${ $item.quantity * $item.price }
```

## Collect results from independent services

If outside services publish events, use `listen.to.all` to require every event type.
Use correlation to scope matches to the current workflow instance.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: listen-for-all-results
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - collectResults:
      listen:
        to:
          all:
            - with:
                type: com.example.inventory.checked
            - with:
                type: com.example.shipping.quoted
      timeout:
        after: PT5M
  - recordResults:
      set:
        checks: ${ . }
```

## Recover when a branch fails

Use `try` around the fork for a group-wide fallback. To recover inside a specific
branch, place the handler in that branch.

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: parallel-checks-with-fallback
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - attemptChecks:
      try:
        - checkOrder:
            fork:
              branches:
                - inventory:
                    call: http
                    with:
                      method: get
                      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/stock
                      query:
                        fail: '503'
                        failTimes: ${ .inventoryFailures // 0 | tostring }
                        key: ${ .orderId }
                - shipping:
                    call: http
                    with:
                      method: post
                      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8787/quotes/express
                      body:
                        orderId: ${ .orderId }
      catch:
        do:
          - requestManualReview:
              set:
                status: needs-review
```

See [Parallel Tasks](lemline-howto-parallel.html) and [Event Correlation](https://github.com/open-workflow-specification/specification/blob/v1.0.3/dsl-reference.md#correlation).

## Run the Examples

Every example on this page is a complete workflow. Complete [the SQLite setup](lemline-tutorial-setup.html), save each example under the file name used below, and run the commands from the setup directory. With the JAR, substitute `java -jar lemline.jar` for `bin/lemline`.

Start the [tutorial shop](lemline-tutorial-order-processing.html#start-the-tutorial-shop) from the root of the Lemline source checkout:

```BASH
docker compose -f examples/tutorial-services/compose.yaml up -d
```

The event examples need the tutorial publisher. Save it as `tutorial-publisher.yaml`:

```YAML
document:
  dsl: '1.0.3'
  namespace: examples
  name: tutorial-publisher
  version: '1.0.0'
do:
  - publish:
      emit:
        event:
          with:
            type: ${ .type }
            source: https://events.example.com/tutorial
            data: ${ .data }
```

Keep the setup worker running and use a second terminal in the setup directory.

```BASH
bin/lemline definition post -f tutorial-publisher.yaml
bin/lemline definition post -f parallel-order-checks.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples parallel-order-checks --input '{"orderId":"QUOTE-1"}'
bin/lemline definition post -f map-order-items.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples map-order-items --input '{"items":[{"id":"SKU-1","quantity":2,"price":25},{"id":"SKU-2","quantity":1,"price":12}]}'
bin/lemline definition post -f listen-for-all-results.yaml
bin/lemline instance start examples listen-for-all-results
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.inventory.checked","data":{"stock":2}}'
bin/lemline instance start examples tutorial-publisher --input '{"type":"com.example.shipping.quoted","data":{"price":15}}'
```
